Listen to this article Share Across university campuses, a new generation of student entrepreneurs is challenging the traditional notion that education ends in the classroom. Armed with innovative ideas, digital skills and an appetite for business, students are increasingly turning their talents into income-generating ventures, creating jobs and building brands while pursuing their degrees. From technology and fashion to food, agriculture and creative industries, campus entrepreneurship is emerging as a powerful driver of innovation, financial independence and economic opportunity, offering a glimpse into the future of youth-led enterprise. Nigeria introduced entrepreneurship education into its university curriculum in 2006 to upskill its teeming youthful population. The rationale for the introduction of entrepreneurship education into the Nigerian university curriculum was to enhance job creation, reduce unemployment, and poverty among young graduates. Nevertheless, the high rate of unemployment, underemployment, and idleness among youth in this dispensation remains a cause for concern. Across various tertiary institutions, entrepreneurial skill acquisition is changing the unemployment narrative, as well as raising innovators and job creators. Asika Eloho, a Master’s degree holder in Entrepreneurship Development and Innovation Management at the University of Lagos, said that beyond academic studies, she is actively involved in entrepreneurship. “My practical experience in business management, baking, product development, marketing, customer relations, and staff management continues to provide valuable opportunities for learning and skills development,” Eloho said. Entrepreneurship, she said, has helped her gain a deeper understanding of business strategy, innovation, funding, scalability, and sustainable enterprise growth. “I’m particularly interested in applying these concepts to improve the structure, efficiency, and growth potential of my bakery. “Through my practical entrepreneurial experience and academic studies, I have developed and strengthened skills in business management, strategic thinking, problem-solving, innovation, financial planning, leadership, and opportunity identification,” she said. Besides, Eloho said that she sees education not just as a means of obtaining qualifications but as a tool for identifying opportunities, solving real-world problems, creating value, and building sustainable businesses. “I have come to appreciate the importance of combining practical experience with theoretical knowledge. Entrepreneurship requires more than passion and hard work; it requires structured planning, sound financial management, innovation, among others,” she said. She emphasized that acquiring business and entrepreneurial skills while on campus is highly valuable because it prepares students for life beyond the classroom. “Entrepreneurial skills help students identify opportunities, develop solutions, and create alternative sources of income. “Students who acquire the skills early can begin testing business ideas, gaining practical experience, and building networks even before graduation,” she noted. Afolabi Sowande, another UNILAG student, said, “My entrepreneurial experience has taught me that practical skills, innovation, and the ability to identify opportunities are just as important as academic knowledge. “I now see education as a tool for building solutions, creating employment, and contributing to economic development rather than simply preparing for paid employment.” Ndumele Chidera, a student of MSc Entrepreneurship Development and Innovation Management at the Entrepreneurship and Skills Development Centre, University of Lagos, buttressed the fact that education goes beyond certificates. “Beyond my academic programme, I’m continuously developing myself through practical experiences, personal learning, business activities, and opportunities that challenge me to think differently. “My training has exposed me to skills in strategic management, marketing, consulting, business analytics, and soft skills, which I believe are valuable across different industries and career paths.” Ajibade Ayodeji, the director of Babcock Entrepreneurship Development Centre (BEDC), said entrepreneurship skills are meant to provide students with practical insights and tools to help them develop their entrepreneurial skills and mindset. “The essence is to inspire and encourage students to become innovative thinkers and problem solvers who can create new businesses, products, and services that address the needs of society,” he said. Experts believe that Nigeria’s next generation of successful startups may increasingly emerge from university campuses, where talent, research, innovation and entrepreneurial ambition converge. However, they say that the universities that will truly lead the pack will be those that move beyond producing graduates to building ecosystems that actively support founders, from providing access to funding, mentorship and industry partnerships to commercialising research and creating pathways for ideas to become scalable businesses.
